result.summary: Neoptolemus, wearing his father Achilles' armour, leads the Greeks into battle and kills Eurypylus in single combat. Ares rallies the Trojans until Athena and Zeus force the gods apart, and the Greeks drive the Trojans behind their walls. Zeus veils Troy in cloud at Ganymede's plea, and the Greeks withdraw for the night.

scenes.title: Neoptolemus Leads the Charge
scenes.summary: At dawn both armies arm. Neoptolemus puts on his father's armour, drives Achilles' horses and cuts down many Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Neoptolemus risks his life, and the Greeks risk their ships and camp, in the first clash with Eurypylus' Trojans.

scenes.title: Heroes Fall on Both Sides
scenes.summary: Aeneas, Diomede, Agamemnon and Meriones each kill a man, while Eurypylus slays many Greeks.
scenes.stakes: Greek warriors face death at the hands of Eurypylus.

scenes.title: Neoptolemus Slays Eurypylus
scenes.summary: The two champions exchange challenges and fight. Neoptolemus kills Eurypylus with his father's spear and scatters the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Each champion fights to the death; Eurypylus loses his life.

scenes.title: Ares and Athena Intervene
scenes.summary: Ares comes in secret to help Troy, and Helenus rallies the Trojans. Many fall on both sides until Athena arrives, and Zeus's thunder drives both gods away.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk rout; Ares and Athena risk Zeus's wrath.

scenes.title: Siege of the Gates
scenes.summary: The Greeks drive the Trojans inside Troy and assault the walls. Meriones kills Phylodamas with an arrow, and Polites escapes a second shot.
scenes.stakes: Troy risks falling; Polites narrowly escapes death.

scenes.title: Zeus Veils Troy; Greeks Withdraw
scenes.summary: Ganymede pleads for his homeland and Zeus hides Troy in cloud. Nestor counsels retreat, and the Greeks bury their dead, wash in the Hellespont and feast; both sides keep watch.
scenes.stakes: Troy would be destroyed without Zeus's intervention; the Greeks fear his wrath.

Ganymede's anguished cry on seeing one's country wrecked by foes.

analysis.text: The book sets a son's inheritance of his father's glory against fate and the gods, who keep deciding the war's course.
Quintus of Smyrna wrote in the Homeric epic tradition, using long similes and divine intervention to continue the Iliad's story.

fun_facts.text: The poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, probably of the 3rd or 4th century AD, and is also called the Posthomerica.

language_notes.text: Achaea is Greece; the Achaeans (Argives) are the Greeks. 'Awelessly' means fearlessly, without dread.
'Mine henchmen' and 'take ye' are archaic: 'my followers' and 'take to heart'. 'Argos' stands for the whole Greek side.
Sirius, the Dog Star, rises in late summer; ancients blamed its heat for fevers and plague. Homer likens Achilles to it too.
Aeacus' son is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus; the steeds judge the young man no worse than their old master.
'Sheen' means brightness, gleam; 'wide space' refers to the plain between wall and ships.
'Welkin' is an archaic word for the sky; 'overpalls' means covers as with a funeral pall.
'Bournes' here means realms or quarters; 'viewless bournes' are unseen regions from which the winds come.
The Trojan allies come from Asia Minor: Caunus, Tarbelus and Imbrus are places in or near Caria and Lycia.
Dardanus is the Trojan region; the bride-bed refers to Anchises' union with Aphrodite (Queen of Love), which produced Aeneas.
"Leal" means loyal; "outfall" is a river's mouth.
"Taslet" (tasset) is armour protecting the thigh; "glancing" means gleaming.
Antiphus is fated to be eaten by the Cyclops Polyphemus, in the Odyssey's tale of Ulysses' companions.
Recalls Achilles wounding Telephus, Eurypylus' father, and later healing him with rust from his spear.
Achilles' immortal horses were sired by the West-wind on the Harpy Podarge, according to myth.
Enyo is a Greek goddess of war who delights in battle's din.
"Seed of Blessed Ones" means descended from gods; both warriors have divine ancestry.
Boreas is the North Wind; Erinys is a Fury. The horses are given a monstrous, storm-born parentage, which explains their fiery breath.
"Cravens" means cowards; "wherefore" means why.
Enyo is a goddess of war, often Ares' companion, named here as a figure moving among the fighters.
Thetis is Achilles' mother, hence Neoptolemus' grandmother. Enyo avoids favouring either side so as not to offend her or Ares.
"Bare" is the old past tense of "bear": Iphianassa gave birth to him.
"Barbs" means the arrowheads; the Fates are said to direct the shaft wherever they wish.
"Wroth" means angry; "scion" in the previous sentence means descendant.
Pallas is another name for Athena, used here in place of the name Athena.
"Battle-fain" means eager for battle; "fain" is archaic for gladly willing or eager.
"Burg" means fortified town; "steading" is a farmstead or sheepfold.
The "Earth-shaker" is Poseidon, who according to legend built Troy's walls, so they are called his divine work.
"Tim Troyfolk" is evidently a misprint for "the Troyfolk", meaning the people of Troy.
"As he listeth" means as he pleases; "scatheless" elsewhere means unharmed.
"Scatheless" means unharmed; "aye waxed" means ever grew.
Argives: Greeks, named for Argos; used throughout as a general name for the Greek army. Ganymedes is the Trojan prince carried off to serve the gods.
"At thine hest" (printed 'best') means at your command; Ganymede claims he left Troy at Zeus's bidding.
Danaans: another name for the Greeks, from Danaus, a legendary king of Argos. Neleus' son is Nestor.
Clarion: a shrill trumpet; here the thunder is likened to a trumpet call.
Refers to Zeus blasting the Titans, the older gods who rebelled against him, with fire, scorching the earth and seas.
Calchas, the Greek seer, prophesied at the muster that Troy would fall in the tenth year of the war.
Hellespont: the strait now called the Dardanelles, beside which the Greek ships were beached.
Thetis is Achilles' sea-goddess mother; here she magically relieves fatigue for her grandson Neoptolemus, the 'valiant son'.

context_notes.text: The Hercules' grandson is Eurypylus, son of Telephus, who came to help Troy and fights Neoptolemus in this book.
The Myrmidons were Achilles' soldiers from Thessaly, now led by his son Neoptolemus.
Thetis was the sea-goddess mother of Achilles; Neoptolemus is her grandson.
Automedon was Achilles' charioteer. The horses were immortal, a gift of the gods to Peleus.
Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, newly arrived at Troy to avenge his father and fight for the Greeks.
Boreas is the North Wind, known for violent storms.
Zeus's thunderbolt is his chief weapon, feared by all the other gods.
Ares, god of war, here favours Troy. The Trojans have been driven back by the Greeks, led by Achilles' son Neoptolemus.
Helenus is a son of Priam and a seer, so he can recognise a god's voice.
Zeus, king of the gods, forbids his divine children to fight each other openly, so he stops the clash with thunder.
Thrace, to the north of Greece, was traditionally the homeland of Ares.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, who joined the Greeks after his father's death and leads them here.
Phoebus is Apollo, who favoured the Trojans throughout the war.
Meriones, son of Molus, is a Cretan archer and a Greek leader.
Enyo is a goddess of war who delights in bloodshed and battle-cries.
Ganymede, a Trojan prince, was taken by Zeus to be cupbearer of the gods and given immortality.
Nestor is the oldest Greek leader, known for wisdom and counsel.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, who has joined the war after his father's death and is now its Greek champion.

literary_notes.text: The Fates are shown standing close by and laughing, making doom feel like a mocking presence.
The Fates' laughter hints that Eurypylus' hopes will fail and he will die.
The hero is compared to the rising sun and Sirius, stressing his dazzling, dangerous radiance.
The Greeks swarming out are likened to angry wasps whose nest has been struck by an axe.
Two armies clashing are compared to opposing winds raising a storm sea, giving the battle elemental scale.
Trojans falling before Neoptolemus are likened to dry brush consumed by wind-driven fire, showing his destructive speed.
Fallen Greeks are compared to felled forest trees, conveying their number and the heavy, chaotic way they drop.
Neoptolemus is likened to a mountain headland unmoved by floods, stressing his unshakable strength.
Starving lions fighting over a carcass capture the savage, desperate ferocity of the two champions.
Strife appears as a spectator gloating over the fighters, making the violence feel presided over by a malign presence.
Eurypylus' fall is likened to an uprooted pine, emphasizing his towering size and the force of his collapse.
Neoptolemus is compared to Zeus's thunderbolt, presenting him as an irresistible, almost divine force.
Fire, Flame, Tumult and Panic are named as Ares' horses, turning abstract terrors into living beings.
Trojans turning back to fight are compared to hounds that rally against a wolf when their shepherd scolds them.
Equal battle is likened to young men pruning a vineyard in step, stressing the even balance of the fighting.
Medon's skill and fair home bring no comfort: he never sees his son again, and kinsmen quarrel over his property.
Neoptolemus killing Trojans is compared to a child swatting flies, showing his ease and his careless delight.
Neoptolemus becomes a mountain peak withstanding hurricanes, conveying his unshaken steadiness against the god-driven Trojans.
Three stacked comparisons, to winds driving ships, fire in brush and hounds chasing deer, convey the Greeks' relentless pursuit.
Trojans penned like lambs suggests helplessness and the Greeks as predatory shepherds.
Greeks compared to starlings swarming an orchard shows their reckless, hungry persistence despite the defenders' efforts.
The falling warrior is likened to a shot vulture, making his sudden plunge from the tower vivid.
The helmsman avoiding a rock mirrors Polites' small, quick movement averting disaster.
The war goddess shouting with glee gives the slaughter a divine, gloating presence.
Ganymede's grief at seeing his kindred and city burn makes the divine plea emotionally intimate.
The wall vanishing like a phantom in mist conveys the sudden, uncanny power of Zeus's intervention.
Nestor's picture of boiling Ocean and dried rivers magnifies Zeus's power to justify retreat.
Dawn that frowns then smiles stands for fortune: present setbacks will turn to success.
The sun driving tireless steeds and night streaming over the earth 'bidding' men rest give natural events divine agency.
